newsitem.title: UK: UK August Purchasing Managers' (PMI) Survey - Text.
newsitem.headline: UK August Purchasing Managers' (PMI) Survey - Text.

text.p: Following is the full text of the August Report on Business (purchasing managers' survey) of the Chartered Institute of Purchasing and Supply (News 2000 subscribers can see separate tables by typing TABLES followed by F9).
MANUFACTURING OUTPUT EXPANDS AT FASTEST RATE IN SIXTEEN MONTHS WHILE PRICES CONTINUE TO FALL
The seasonally adjusted Purchasing Managers' Index* rose to its highest level in a year in August. Both output and new order levels expanded more rapidly than at any time since the spring of 1995.

This suggests that the slowdown in manufacturing activity, which began in late-1994, probably bottomed out in May. Since then, rising consumers' expenditure has been the main driving force behind steadily accelerating growth in the manufacturing sector. In August the survey also found increasing evidence that the strengthened demand for consumer goods has begun to feed down the supply chain. Most notable was the impact upon producers of intermediate goods, many of whom supply components to the consumer goods sector. These suppliers saw their warehouse stocks of unsold goods fall very sharply for the third month running in August. In order to restock warehouses and meet higher demand, output of intermediate goods rose sharply. The consumer goods' industries saw a corresponding lengthening of delivery times for certain components, reflecting the need for suppliers to meet demand by raising output due to insufficient warehouse stock.

The Delivery Times Index fell to its lowest level since last September as a result, but nevertheless continued to show a very slight shortening of average lead-times across all sectors. This suggests that total demand remained relatively weak by historical standards, a fact linked by panel members to the continuation of intense price competition among suppliers. Nearly a quarter of all companies saw prices fall whereas only 6% saw prices rise.

Conditions remain particularly weak for investment/capital goods, and producers in this sector continued to focus upon running down finished goods' stock by cutting production. Nevertheless, the severe deterioration in orders for investment goods which occurred in the first half of the year appears to have bottomed out, suggesting that firms in the consumer and intermediate goods sectors have begun to increase their capital expenditures.

Employment remained relatively unchanged, however, as the take up of full time staff was reported to have been generally subdued by continued uncertainty about future order levels. * The Purchasing Managers' Index (PMI) is a composite indicator designed to provide an overall view of activity in the manufacturing economy. The indicator is derived from individual diffusion indices which measure changes in output, new orders, employment, suppliers' delivery times and stocks of goods purchased.

A reading of the PMI below 50% indicates that the manufacturing economy is generally declining; above 50%, that it is generally expanding. The seasonally adjusted index may be subject to revision as improved estimation of seasonal adjustments occur with each month's new data.
OUTPUT

The seasonally adjusted Output Index rose to its highest level since April 1995 and signalled an increase in the rate of growth of production. In recent months the strongest growth had been recorded by producers of consumer goods, but in August the fastest growth was recorded in the intermediate goods' industries, who have benefited from the increased demand for components used in the production of consumer goods.
NEW ORDERS

The rate of growth of new orders was unchanged on July, but over the past three months the overall level has been stronger than at any time since March 1995. Orders for consumer goods continued to rise, with this growth feeding through to their suppliers (producers of intermediate goods). Meanwhile orders for investment goods also showed tentative signs of growth, rising very marginally for the second month running.
QUANTITY OF PURCHASES

Having fallen in each of the past ten months, the amount of goods bought by purchasing managers was unchanged in August, after seasonal factors had been accounted for. Whereas producers of consumer goods increased their purchases to meet faster output growth, producers of intermediate and investment goods continued to focus upon keeping stock levels to a minimum and consequently cut back on their purchasing.
PRICES

The Prices Index rose in August, but remains at a very low level by this survey's historical standards. Just under a quarter of all companies saw the average price paid for their purchases fall. In general, weak worldwide demand for many goods -- both commodities and semi-manufactures -- continued to drive price competition among suppliers.
SUPPLIERS' DELIVERY TIMES

The Suppliers' Delivery Times Index, at 50.3, registered its lowest level since September last year. Over 12% of companies surveyed saw slower delivery times, suggesting that demand has tightened in some markets and suppliers have become busier. This was particularly evident for the supply of semi-manufactured (intermediate) goods rather than commodities.
STOCKS OF PURCHASES

Stock levels fell to a lesser extent than in any month since March. As in recent months, where stocks fell it was largely intentional. General good availability of supplies, combined with widespread price competition among suppliers, has allowed purchasing managers to hold low stock levels. However, the rise in the index was caused by a rise in stocks in the investment goods sector due to falling usage in production.
STOCKS OF FINISHED GOODS

On the whole, stocks of finished goods fell. Producers of investment goods generally cut output and chose to meet sales from stock in order to clear warehouse shelves. For intermediate goods, on the other hand, a sharp fall in stocks was associated with stronger than expected demand in addition to such deliberate destocking policies. In the production of consumer goods, however, some signs of restocking appeared.
EMPLOYMENT

The Employment Index rose to a level above 50.0 for only the second time this year, but at 50.1 this merely suggests a flat picture. The incidence of redundancies fell compared with July but take up of permanent staff was generally reported to have remained subdued by continued uncertainty about future business prospects.
INDICES BY MARKET SECTOR
CONSUMER GOODS

New orders for consumer goods rose again in August, from both home and export markets. Although the rate of order book growth has steadily slowed since June, growth remained sufficiently strong to encourage producers of consumer goods to increase their rate of production. This led to the first (small) rise in stocks of finished goods since January. Stocks of purchased goods were deliberately allowed to fall, reflecting an increase in just in time purchasing and production. Producers were able to hold lower stocks due to the improved availability of goods and confidence over future prices (continued price competition among suppliers was widespread). Employment rose only slightly, although this was largely due to the slow take up of seasonal labour.
INVESTMENT GOODS INDUSTRIES

The New Orders Index for capital goods, such as plant and machinery, remained marginally higher than 50.0 for the second month running in August, suggesting that the decline in order books seen over the previous five months may have bottomed out. But the Output Index dropped to its lowest level since September 1992 in August as companies met existing demand from stock rather than higher output. This was intentional in order to reduce stocks of finished goods, which fell accordingly. Purchasing managers also bought fewer materials compared with July, reflecting continued efforts to reduce these stocks in line with current low output levels. The Employment Index rose, however, reflecting increased optimism about future business levels.
INTERMEDIATE GOODS

Production of intermediate goods rose to its highest level since April 1995 in August, the third consecutive monthly increase following a poor first half to the year. A considerable contribution to the increase was a rise in orders from producers of consumer goods, whose requirements have risen with the strengthened market for these goods. Stocks of purchases were more than adequate to meet the increase in output, and purchasing was deliberately cut in order to let these stocks fall. Stocks of finished goods also fell, the largest fall since the survey began. This fall reflected further destocking polices, but also depletion through strong sales. Employment fell, but this was largely due to weakness of the temporary, rather than permanent, labour market.
PRICE CHANGES/SUPPLY SHORTAGES

Purchasing managers generally found supply to have exceeded demand for most products, although the number of non-food items reported to have been in short supply rose slightly compared with a month ago. For most goods, therefore, price competition among suppliers led to falling prices. However, some firms have begun to see some price rises.
PAPER AND TIMBER

Paper is a key market for providing an early indication of the strength of general manufacturing demand conditions. For the second month running, some tightening of the paper market was found, with several cases of paper and pulp lead-times lengthening as demand picks up. Pulp rose in price for the fourth consecutive month. On the whole, however, these were isolated instances and prices continued to fall for most paper and paper-based packaging products.
METALS

Prices for a wide variety of metals -- including steel, aluminium and copper -- continued to fall in line with LME rates, generally reflecting weak world-wide demand. Very few cases of metals, or metal-based goods, rising in price were found, although stainless and galvanised steel shortages were reported.
ELECTRONIC/ELECTRICAL
The number of electrical/electronic items found to have been in short supply rose in August, but prices generally continued to fall.
PLASTICS
Slow sales, especially in Europe, have led to falling prices for many plastics, notable PVC, which has now fallen in price for 14 successive months.
CHEMICALS
The availability of all chemicals except silocon remained good.
RUBBER
Natural rubber generally continued to drop in price (the ninth month running). But, for the second time in three months, some firms faced higher rubber prices as demand strengthened.
